newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia cannot meet own investment needs - report.
newsitem.headline: Russia cannot meet own investment needs - report.

text.p: Russia is not able to meet its commercial investment needs and must turn to foreign capital, Russian Economic Trends said on Wednesday in a new report.
"Given the huge requirements and the low level of domestic savings, the large shortfall in funds will have to come largely from abroad," it said.

Capital stock, or the value of all company assets, was declining, it said, adding, "given that investment dropped in real terms by 10 percent in 1995 and 18 percent in 1996, it seems that this trend has continued and even accelerated."
But the government's share of private sector assets, expected to decline with the sharp fall in yields on government securities to 20 percent from about 200 percent last year, is growing.
As a result, bank assets channeled into private sector loans were unchanged over the last year, while foreign holdings in the T-bill and domestic bond market appear to be about 40 percent.

Bank assets in loans to the government rose steadily to 6.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) or 164 trillion roubles ($28 billion) in February from 3.8 percent of GDP or 78 trillion roubles in February 1996.
Over that period, loans to the private sector by the banks fell to 6.5 percent of GDP or 167 trillion roubles from 6.8 percent or 140 trillion roubles, it quoted central bank figures as showing.

Household savings are relatively small -- the four percent savings rate is about the same as the U.S. -- and the rate of growth of household deposits will probably slow this year, given lower interest rates on government securities, it said.
